title: Tiny Diamond Anvils Reveal Iron Minerals That Could Store Earth's Primordial Water
summary: Earth's mantle is a roughly 3,000-kilometer-thick layer of slowly flowing rock between the crust and the core. Scientists know there's water down there, but exactly how it's stored and moved has been a mystery. Now, researchers have discovered two new iron minerals — called iron oxyhydroxides — that can hold water at the extreme temperatures and pressures found near the core-mantle boundary, where pressure is more than a million times what we feel at the surface. The team created the minerals by squeezing samples between two tiny diamond anvils while zapping them with a laser. The new minerals contain as much as 15% water by weight. "If you add up all the H and O atoms in the formula and combine them into H2O, just a five-pound piece of the stuff would contain a pint of liquid water," said Steve Jacobsen, a mineralogist at the University of Colorado Boulder who was not involved in the study. That water matters because it makes mantle rock stretchier and able to flow. This convection is a big reason Earth has plate tectonics — without water, the mantle would be too stiff to drag the crust around. There are two leading theories for how water enters the mantle. One is subduction: when a tectonic plate sinks beneath another, it carries surface water down with it. The other is primordial water, left over from Earth's formation and stored near the core-mantle boundary. The new minerals fit both theories. They are dense enough to sink all the way to the bottom of the mantle, and strong enough to survive the high-energy impacts of early Earth. Mantle plumes could later carry them upward, where they would melt and release water, contributing to volcanic hotspots. The study, published Sept. 8 in Nature Geoscience, doesn't prove these minerals are actively transporting water today. But knowing they exist provides a pathway for the first time. The minerals might also explain mysterious, ultra-dense patches sitting on top of the core-mantle boundary. And they could help scientists understand water cycles on other rocky planets and exoplanets — especially molten ones.
why_it_matters: If water can be locked into minerals and carried thousands of kilometres through the mantle, then Earth's water budget is not fixed at the surface — it circulates on geological timescales, and that circulation helps keep plate tectonics running. The same chemistry may decide whether rocky exoplanets can hold onto oceans, which directly shapes the search for habitable worlds.

background_read: The idea that Earth's outer shell is broken into moving plates — plate tectonics — was only widely accepted in the 1960s, decades after Alfred Wegener's earlier idea of continental drift had been dismissed.
The engine behind it is convection in the mantle: hot rock rises, cooler rock sinks, and water is what makes the rock soft enough to move at all.
Scientists have already found a water-rich mineral called ringwoodite trapped inside diamonds that formed deep underground, direct evidence that the deep mantle can store water rather than just rock.

The core-mantle boundary (the border, thousands of kilometres down, where the iron core meets the rocky mantle) is one of the least understood regions of the planet, and the authors suggest these minerals may help explain the ultra-dense patches sitting there.

Nature Geoscience (a peer-reviewed journal that publishes research on the solid Earth, its atmosphere and other planets) published the study, which used laboratory experiments rather than samples from the deep Earth.
The work also reaches outward: astronomers now study rocky exoplanets, and whether a planet can lock water inside its interior may help decide whether it could ever have had oceans or life.

perspectives.description: For the first time there is a plausible mineral pathway for storing water right at the core-mantle boundary, which also offers an explanation for the mysterious ultra-dense patches detected there. It connects lab chemistry to real seismic structures, which is rare and valuable.

The minerals were made in the lab in minutes, while the real mantle has had billions of years to react, and nobody has yet found these phases in actual deep-Earth samples. Until there is independent evidence from seismology or geochemistry, the transport idea remains a hypothesis, not a demonstrated process.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — an old debate gets a new candidate
perspectives.description: The question of whether deep water comes from subducted surface water or from Earth's original building blocks has been argued for years, and the minerals fit both stories. That may mean the two sources operate together rather than one replacing the other.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — where the field goes next
perspectives.description: Testing the idea will require matching lab data to seismic signals and searching for these phases in natural samples, perhaps in diamonds that formed deep underground. If it holds up, the same framework could be applied to other rocky planets and molten exoplanets, where interior water may control climate and habitability.
